newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Britain in dock at EU agriculture meet over BSE.
newsitem.headline: Britain in dock at EU agriculture meet over BSE.

text.p: Britain, the European Union's persistent delinquent, was in the dock again on Sunday as EU Agriculture ministers gathered to discuss London's refusal to carry out proposed steps to end the mad cow disease crisis.

The four-day meeting, which was supposed to be a relaxed and informal gathering, will be dominated by Britain's refusal to carry out a cattle cull agreed at an EU Florence summit in June as part of a plan to end a ban on British beef exports.

Irish Agriculture Minister Ivan Yates, the meeting's host under Ireland's six-month EU presidency, said this week that he would do all he could to prevent the standoff turning into a re-run of a crisis which partly paralysed EU business in June.

"I want to make it clear that the Irish presidency will try to do everything in the dialogue between the European Commission, the EU and Britain to try and reconstruct a basis to proceed," he told Irish radio.
Agriculture ministers were due to arrive in this southern Irish town later on Sunday for a programme which includes visits to selected Irish farms and traditional hospitality.

But working sessions and informal discusssions are expected to be dominated by a crisis which has dogged EU business since Britain announced in March that a fatal brain-wasting disease could be caught by people who ate BSE-infected beef.

The EU Commission banned British beef exports and Britain retaliated by refusing to co-operate in EU decision-making, causing a crisis that was thought to have been defused with a package of measures agreed at the June Florence summit.
Britain has suspended the planned cull because of domestic research suggesting that mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) would die out naturally in five years.

Britain's Conservative government under Prime Minister John Major is under intense domestic pressure from the farm lobby and right-wingers not to go ahead with the cull and faces calls from "Eurosceptics" in his party to get tough with Europe.

The row, coupled with Britain's go-it-alone attitude in other areas of EU business ranging from a single currency to a common security policy, has sorely stretched the patience of other EU member states.
The President of the European Parliament, Klaus Haensch, even suggested last week that if Britain did not like the rules of the EU club it had joined, it should leave.
"If the British abandon the Union's internal solidarity, when they don't respect decisions taken together, they they do not belong in the Union," he said.
The EU Farm Commissioner, Franz Fischler, said that there was nothing new in the British scientific data but is expecting British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg to explain it.

"As long as they (Britain) do not meet the pre-conditions and until we have a working document from them which we can carefully check, then an end to the export ban is simply not a possibility," he told the European Parliament.
EU Commission President Jacques Santer said in remarks published in Belgium at the weekend that Britain should play a more constructive role in the bloc.
"A large country like Britain has every interest in participating in a direct, conscious and constructive way in this big European adventure," he told the daily Le Soir. REUTER
